title: Delta-Doped GeV$^-$ in diamond with isotope resolvable optical spectra
authors: Ian N. Hammock, Kinfung Ngan, Antoni W. Wellisz, Keira Linder, Midrel Wilfried Ngandeu Ngambou, Jiefei Zhang, Xinghan Guo, Benjamin Pingault, Shuo Sun, David D. Awschalom, F. Joseph Heremans, Alexander A. High, Nazar Delegan
abstract: Group IV color centers in diamond -- silicon, germanium, tin, and lead-vacancy centers -- are a promising platform for quantum networking. Typical Group-IV creation utilizes ion implantation during diamond growth that leaves the color centers with a broad depth distribution and damage-induced strain inhomogeneity. Deterministic placement and damage reduction in Group IV generation are essential for improving this platform. In this letter, we report on the localization of germanium-vacancy (GeV$^-$) to a $<$ 10 nm layer via the timed injection of GeH$_4$ during microwave plasma chemical vapor deposition. In this layer we have realized 17 ppm of Ge and a strain-free environment for the GeV$^-$. Subsequent electron irradiation and annealing have generated a sheet density of 0.12 GeV$^-$/$μ$m$^2$. The minimal damage from color center generation mitigates spectral inhomogeneity and allows spectral resolution of isotopic clusters, with the best cluster having an inhomogeneous distribution of 2.14 GHz and an average linewidth of $47 \pm 11$ MHz. Our study gives insight into formation dynamics of GeV$^-$ in delta-doped systems and estimates our vacancy to GeV$^-$ yield to be $\geq$ 90%, establishing an athermal nearest-neighbor formation model. We further characterized the spin $T_2^*$ and set a lower bound of 730 ns, limited by a paramagnetic defect.
summary: This paper reports on the creation of high-quality, delta-doped Germanium-Vacancy ($	ext{GeV}^-$) centers in diamond using controlled plasma deposition and irradiation. The authors achieved excellent spectral homogeneity and a measurable spin coherence time, confirming that the formation process is dominated by athermal mechanisms. This work establishes a scalable platform for solid-state quantum memory applications.
main_problem: The primary challenge is improving the deterministic placement and reducing damage in Group-IV color centers (like $	ext{GeV}^-$) in diamond for use in quantum networking.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated the creation of a high-quality sheet of $	ext{GeV}^-$ centers with minimal strain, achieving a spin coherence time ($T_2^*$) lower bound of $730 	ext{ ns}$.
method: The research combines advanced material growth techniques (MPCVD) for precise doping, followed by controlled electron irradiation and annealing to generate the color centers.
model_or_system: The system is the $	ext{GeV}^-$ color center in diamond, which is engineered via delta-doping of Germanium. The formation process is modeled as predominantly athermal, involving direct displacement of a carbon atom neighboring a substitutional germanium site ($	ext{Ges}$).
key_observables: Spectral linewidths ($47 \pm 11 	ext{ MHz}$), spin coherence time ($T_2^*$), orbital splitting ($\approx 160 	ext{ GHz}$), and $	ext{GeV}^-$ sheet density ($0.12 	ext{ GeV}^-/\mu	ext{m}^2$).
important_parameters: Ge layer depth localization ($< 10 	ext{ nm}$), $	ext{GeV}^-$ yield ($\ge 90\%$), and the limiting factor for $T_2^*$ attributed to a paramagnetic defect.
main_assumptions: The $	ext{GeV}^-$ creation is assumed to be driven by athermal processes, and the spin coherence limitation is attributed to an unknown paramagnetic defect.
figures_summary: Figures detail PL spectra showing isotopic clustering, orbital splitting histograms confirming low strain, and EPR spectra confirming the $g \approx 2$ resonance associated with even Ge isotopes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the material platform via controlled doping (MPCVD) to generating the centers via irradiation, characterizing the resulting optical and spin properties (PLE, CPT, EPR), and finally discussing the physical mechanisms governing formation and decoherence.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the engineering requirements for solid-state quantum memories and quantum interconnects by providing unprecedented control over defect placement and spectral purity in a solid-state host.
